title: 'Do We Want to Deport Foreign Doctors?' CEO Challenges H-1B Grace-Period Repeal
excerpt: Seattle immigration-firm CEO Xiao Wang says a Department of Homeland Security proposal to scrap the 60-day grace period for laid-off H-1B workers would force foreign doctors and engineers out of the country immediately — even when another employer wants to hire them.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period that lets laid-off H-1B and other employment-based visa holders find a new sponsoring employer, change status, or prepare to leave the United States.
  • Xiao Wang, CEO of a Seattle-based immigration firm, warned the change would force out foreign doctors whose hospitals close and AI engineers whose startups fold — even when another employer is ready to hire them.
  • Wang said even the existing 60-day window is inadequate in this job market: finding a new position that comes with visa sponsorship within two months is a tall order.
  • The proposal is not yet law. The notice of proposed rulemaking was published in the Federal Register and is open to public comment; the grace period remains in place for now.
  • The proposal lands amid broader H-1B tightening, including a new $100,000 fee on each new H-1B petition and a wage-weighted lottery that has cut selection odds for entry-level roles such as medical residents.

"Do we want to deport foreign doctors?" The question, posed by the CEO of a Seattle-based immigration firm, captures the sharpest edge of a Department of Homeland Security proposal that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based visa holders who lose their jobs. Xiao Wang asked whether the United States is prepared to lose members of its medical profession — and senior AI engineers — because a new rule leaves them no time between a layoff and departure.

Under the proposal, workers whose employment ends would generally be expected to leave the U.S. at once unless they already have another lawful basis to stay. There would be no bridge period to find a new sponsoring employer, change immigration status, or wind down a life. Wang argued the rule would punish precisely the workers the U.S. should want to keep.

Two thought experiments

Wang presented two scenarios as thought experiments. A foreign doctor is working at a hospital that shuts down. A senior AI engineer is at a startup that folds. Both can readily find new jobs, he said — hospitals and tech companies are hiring — but the proposed rule does not give them any time to look for one. Instead, they would have to pack their bags and leave the country.

https://x.com/96Stats/status/2098641224437465261

"Imagine losing your job and being told you may also need to leave the country immediately: leases, mortgages, kids' school, years or decades of your life all instantly upended."

— Xiao Wang, CEO of a Seattle-based immigration firm

That abrupt upending is what thousands of foreign workers could face, Wang said — and even the existing 60 days is barely enough when the new job must come with visa sponsorship.

A workforce the health system depends on

The medical profession is where the stakes of the proposal are most visible. Roughly one in four U.S. physicians is an international medical graduate, and foreign-trained doctors disproportionately staff primary care practices in poor and rural communities. About 20.8 million Americans live in areas where at least half of the physicians are foreign-trained, according to data cited by the American Medical Association, and more than 85 million live in designated primary-care shortage areas. The Health Resources and Services Administration projects a shortfall of more than 70,600 primary care physicians by 2038.

The grace-period proposal is one of several pressures on these doctors. The administration imposed a $100,000 fee on each new H-1B petition — up from about $3,500 — which rural and underserved hospitals say they cannot afford. A wage-weighted lottery introduced in February has tilted selection toward senior roles, cutting projected odds for entry-level applicants such as medical residents to roughly 15 percent. The White House has signaled case-by-case "national interest" exemptions for physicians, but none have been publicly reported.

Indian nationals form the largest share of H-1B holders and the deepest green-card backlog among foreign physicians, with many waiting years for permanent residency — so a rule that turns any layoff into an immediate departure order would fall hardest on them.

What happens next

For now, the proposal remains just that. The notice of proposed rulemaking published in the Federal Register is open to public comment, and the 60-day grace period remains in effect. "The good news is nothing has changed yet," Wang said. "But it's yet another signal from this administration to be unreasonable to the detriment of people's lives and overall economic prosperity."

The $100,000 H-1B fee is already facing legal challenges, and worker advocates, hospital systems, and universities are expected to flood the comment period before any final rule takes shape.
